chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah narrated from Abdullah ibn Jabalah, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Hamzah ibn Humran, from Abdullah al-Hamid al-Ta'i, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, the seller of calanises (woolen cloaks), who said:

A man entrusted something to me and left five hundred or six hundred dirhams, and he had a daughter. He told me that there were agnates (asabah) in Syria. So I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that, and he said, 'Give the daughter half and the agnates half.'

When I arrived in Kufa, I informed our companions of his saying, and they said, 'Be careful of him (or: Fear that he might be testing you), so give the daughter the other half.' Then I performed Hajj and met Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and I informed him of what my companions said, and I informed him that I had given the other half to his daughter. He said, 'You did well. I only gave you the ruling fearing the agnates might claim against you.'

key_terms.اَلْعَصَبَة: Agnates (male relatives who inherit the residue of the estate)

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between fixed inheritance shares and precautionary rulings in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the distinction between *al-hukm al-zahir* (apparent ruling) and *al-hukm al-batin* (hidden ruling) in Shia jurisprudence, where Imam al-Sadiq (AS) advised a provisional distribution to avoid conflict with the agnates (*al-‘asabah*) rather than stating the final fixed share. It demonstrates the pragmatic application of *khalaf al-ghalib* (probability) in legal rulings, showing how Imams tailored instructions to social realities while preserving the underlying legal truth. This case is frequently cited to explain why certain hadiths may appear to contradict others when one considers the context of precaution (*ihtiyat*) versus definitive decree (*hukm mu’tamad*).
